title: Pali, closed
hookLine: back from a month abroad with thank you, sorry and a bus stop: what is a little of a language worth?
tomorrow: a monk says he wrote a poem only for himself. so why read it?

lines: THANK YOU, SORRY, A BUS STOP.
cards: Someone comes home from a month abroad and can't order a full meal in the language. But they can say thank you, and sorry, and the name of their bus stop, and the woman at the bakery smiles every time. That's not fluency.
It isn't nothing, either. Twenty-nine days of Pali come to something like that. So, one question to close the block: what is a little of an old language actually worth?

teach.h: LEARN IT IN YOUR OWN DIALECT.
teach.b: The tradition's answer starts where this block did. When two monks asked to put the teaching into grand verse, the Buddha said no: learn it in your own dialect. Meaning comes first.
It's a shared door, the tongue the chants live in, so a girl from a Vietnamese family can chant beside Lao kids and Thai grandparents and all of them land on the same word.
Look what's behind that door now: namo, homage; saranam, refuge; sikkhapada, a training taken up. The heart in Pali. Come and see.
Thus indeed is he. Practicing well. Skilled in good.
The highest blessing. Thus have I heard. Sadhu.
Strive on with care. A little Pali. Now a neighbor.
A Muslim friend who grew up speaking Urdu or English or Malay may still say alhamdulillah, praise be to God, after a meal or a sneeze or good news.

It comes from the Qur'an's opening chapter, in Pickthall's words: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." A few old words, carried into ordinary days by people of different mother tongues. That's shared.

teach.h: GOD'S OWN WORD, OR ANY DIALECT.
teach.b: Muslims hold the Qur'an's Arabic to be God's own revealed word, which is why recitation keeps it.
In the Pali story, the Buddha let his words go out in any dialect, and Buddhism names no God speaking them. Same door-sized words. Different houses behind them.

how: Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Laos and beyond chant in Pali while speaking their own languages at home; new chanters learn by ear, a few words at a time, sometimes from sheets with a translation alongside.

games.q: your uncle says learning a few Pali lines is pointless unless you can read the whole canon. what's the tradition's best answer?
o: he's right: it only counts once you're fluent.
meaning first, in your own words; a little Pali is a shared door into the chants and the people.
the Pali sounds work by themselves, so understanding doesn't matter.
games.why: the Buddha let monks learn in their own dialect, so meaning leads; Pali stays as the common tongue of the chants, a door, not a password.

practice: Chant the homage once more, slowly: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. Then listen to the quiet right after it, the way a bell's sound thins out. Stay with that one sound until it's gone, and then with the stillness.

wordCard.voice: Pali: the language of the Theravada chants and canon. Not a password; a shared door, learned a few words at a time.

orig.note: Pali in Devanagari letters: the name of the language the Theravada chants are kept in.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a little Pali, a door that opens onto people. The block is complete.
